column1: What is 'level-triggered reconciliation' in Kubernetes, and how does it differ from edge-triggered (imperative) orchestration?
column2: Level-triggered reconciliation continuously re-evaluates and re-applies intent, acting on the persistent gap between desired and actual state forever. Edge-triggered orchestration executes a command once and forgets, assuming success without ongoing verification.

column1: What is the quorum formula for Raft consensus given N replicas, and why do production etcd clusters always use odd numbers?
column2: Q = ⌊N/2⌋ + 1. Odd-numbered clusters are used because an even-numbered cluster (e.g., 4) requires the same quorum as the next lower odd cluster (3), so the extra node adds no additional fault tolerance—just wasted redundancy.

column1: Why does the quorum intersection property prevent split-brain in a Raft-based system?
column2: Any two majority quorums out of N nodes must share at least one common node (combinatorial inevitability), so a read quorum always intersects a prior write quorum, preventing two disjoint subsets from independently accepting conflicting state.

column1: In etcd's MVCC model, does the global revision counter increment once per key modified or once per transaction?
column2: Once per committed Raft log entry (transaction), regardless of how many keys are modified within that transaction.

column1: What does the Kubernetes `resourceVersion` field on an API object actually represent?
column2: It is the etcd revision number at which that object was last modified, used for optimistic concurrency control—clients must supply the expected revision to detect conflicting updates (mismatch yields HTTP 409 Conflict).

column1: What consistency guarantee does etcd provide, and what does it formally mean (per Herlihy and Wing, 1990)?
column2: Linearizability: every operation appears to take effect atomically at some single instant between its invocation and its response, visible identically to all subsequent operations—stronger than sequential or eventual consistency.

column1: In the Kubernetes API server request pipeline, what is the strict ordering of security stages a request must pass through before reaching etcd?
column2: Transport Security (mTLS) → Authentication → Authorization → Admission Control (Mutating then Validating) → etcd persistence. Failure at any stage rejects the request (401, 403, or 400) with no bypass.

column1: In X.509 client certificate authentication for Kubernetes, how are username and group membership derived from the certificate?
column2: The CN (Common Name) field maps to the username; the O (Organization) fields map to group memberships.

column1: What is the ownership hierarchy between a Deployment, ReplicaSet, and Pod, and why does this layering matter?
column2: Deployment owns ReplicaSet(s), which own Pod(s). A Deployment never directly manages Pods; each template change creates a new ReplicaSet, enabling rolling updates and rollbacks by scaling old vs. new ReplicaSets.

column1: Why must Kubernetes controllers be idempotent, and what practical behavior does this guarantee enable?
column2: Because reconciliation continuously reapplies desired state, idempotency ensures applying the same spec multiple times causes no additional side effects—this is why `kubectl apply` is safe to run repeatedly.

column1: What storage structure does etcd use to persist versioned key history, and what operation reclaims old versions?
column2: An append-only B+ tree stores each key's ordered sequence of immutable versions tagged by revision; old versions are discarded only via an explicit compaction operation.

column1: What single invariant underlies Kubernetes' entire control plane correctness model, expressed as a reconciliation function?
column2: desired_state(t) = f(spec) and reconcile(observed_state, desired_state) → Δ_actions — controllers continuously compute and close the delta between desired and observed state.
